I am focusing on identifying the specific thresholds for free and pay-as-you-go plans, particularly looking for shifts in how high-throughput models are prioritized relative to the more reasoning-intensive variants. A key part of my synthesis will be resolving any discrepancies between documented ceilings and the actual performance metrics observed in recent technical releases to provide a realistic view of throughput capabilities.

I intend to analyze recent update logs to pinpoint any trajectory shifts in context window capacities and latency optimizations that have occurred over the past several months, ensuring the report reflects the most recent infrastructure upgrades.

I have synthesized a clear picture of the current ecosystem where Gemini 3.5 Flash and 3.1 Flash-Lite serve as the primary accessible models. A major shift occurred in early 2026 when the most advanced reasoning models were moved exclusively to paid tiers, leaving the free environment for high-efficiency, lower-latency tasks. I’ve also identified that 'thinking' tokens—the computational steps used for complex reasoning—are now explicitly billed as output, which is a critical detail for cost estimation in agent-based workflows.

**Resolving Platform Discrepancies**

I am currently thinking through several contradictions in the reported service limits for high-volume users. Some data suggests that spending caps for mid-level and top-level tiers appear identical in some documentation, which might indicate a transition point where users move from standard tiers to custom enterprise agreements. I am also tracking the emergence of a new unified platform mentioned in recent updates, as it appears to be replacing older management tools and could significantly alter how these models are integrated into applications.

**Mapping Performance and Technical Architecture**

My next priority is to investigate specific timing benchmarks and throughput capacities that define the user experience across different model versions. I plan to analyze technical documentation to extract exact volume limits for the paid service levels and search for any available data regarding the underlying model scales. I will also be looking to clarify the transition path to the newly announced unified platform to ensure my final synthesis includes the most current integration standards.

**Evolving Model Hierarchy and Unified Platforms**

I have identified a significant shift in the model landscape as of mid-2026, where high-speed, efficiency-focused variants are now outperforming reasoning-heavy models in specific coding and agentic benchmarks. My investigation reveals that the legacy command-line interface is being phased out in favor of the 'Antigravity' platform, a unified environment designed for multi-agent orchestration. Additionally, I've confirmed that reasoning models were removed from free access tiers earlier this year, establishing a clearer distinction between developer experimentation and high-performance production workloads.

**Reconciling Performance Metrics and Tiered Capacity**

A key complexity I am currently resolving involves the discrepancy between documented performance and observed throughput; while technical benchmarks suggest speeds of up to 183 tokens per second for high-efficiency models, I need to verify if these are officially guaranteed service levels. Furthermore, while I have gathered data on batch processing limits for various paid tiers, the specific real-time request and token-per-minute ceilings for high-volume users remain partially obscured, necessitating a deeper look into tier-based scaling behaviors.

**Mapping Infrastructure Quotas and Migration Paths**

I am now moving to synthesize the impact of the new agent-first platform on existing API integrations and will focus on extracting precise enterprise cloud quotas across different regions. My next phase involves clarifying the exact context window limits—specifically whether the rumored 2-million-token capacity has moved beyond the preview stage—and detailing the spend-based restriction mechanisms that manage rolling usage windows for high-frequency applications.

**Mapping Throughput Ceilings**

I have successfully mapped the specific throughput ceilings for different service levels, identifying that top-tier accounts can now access baseline capacities of up to 10 million tokens per minute for the newest high-efficiency models. This represents a massive scaling path from entry-level paid plans, which typically start with a 300 request-per-minute limit, providing a clear trajectory for applications moving into high-volume production. I've also confirmed that while certain trial tiers were removed for advanced models earlier this year, the remaining high-speed variants still offer a foundational access point for initial testing.

**Context Scaling and Caching**

I am analyzing a significant shift in long-context processing, where flagship reasoning models have stabilized at a two-million-token window. My synthesis reveals that this capability is paired with a tiered pricing model that offers a 90% discount on cached data, effectively changing the architectural strategy for analyzing massive repositories. While some platforms use shared throughput tiers, others maintain a strict system limit of 30,000 requests per minute per region. This framework moves beyond simple request-response cycles to support server-side conversation state and background execution for long-running tasks. My analysis confirms that while older methods remain supported, all frontier capabilities—particularly those involving autonomous tool use and complex reasoning chains—are now optimized exclusively for this new standard.

I am currently resolving a discrepancy in technical specifications regarding maximum response lengths, as recent documentation alternates between 64,000 and 65,536 tokens for the latest high-efficiency models. Furthermore, I am investigating a potential conflict between two distinct resource models: a token-based tier system for direct developer access and a credit-based subscription model used by the unified management platform. Defining how these two paradigms overlap is essential for accurate capacity planning in large-scale deployments.

I’ve also observed that the high-efficiency 'Lite' variants have reached a significant speed milestone of 350 tokens per second, making them the primary choice for high-throughput real-time applications as of mid-2026.

This shift signals a move away from simple stateless requests toward managed conversation states and orchestration. Furthermore, I am investigating an ambiguity in the top-tier spending restrictions; while some sources suggest a two-hundred-dollar rolling window cap, I need to confirm if higher custom ceilings exist for the most demanding enterprise deployments to provide an accurate capacity model.

My next phase involves synthesizing the precise technical specifications for the new interaction framework to ensure a clear understanding of its metadata requirements. I will also focus on clarifying the conversion mechanisms between platform credits and raw API tokens, which is essential for accurate cost-benefit analysis. Once I have reconciled the throughput limits for the highest usage levels, I will be ready to provide a definitive overview of the current resource landscape.

**Tier Scaling and Model Transitions**

I have identified the specific scaling path for production accounts, where the most advanced tier now provides a ceiling of 4,000 requests per minute and a daily capacity of 50,000 calls. This accompanies a major ecosystem shift where the legacy 1.5 and 2.0 model families were fully retired this summer, consolidating all active development onto the newest high-efficiency versions and ensuring that current workloads leverage the latest architectural improvements.

**Solidifying Usage Safeguards**

My analysis has clarified how usage is governed beyond simple token counts, uncovering a specific $200 spending limit evaluated over a rolling ten-minute window for high-volume users. This effectively balances massive throughput capabilities with real-time budget protection, ensuring that even the most aggressive agentic loops remain within predefined financial boundaries while maintaining high-frequency performance.

**Validating Integration Protocols**

I am now prioritizing the retrieval of the exact data structures required for the newest stateful communication standard to ensure technical accuracy for the final report. Additionally, I will investigate if the most recent model updates have adjusted the eligibility requirements for automatic tier upgrades to provide a clear roadmap for users moving from initial testing to large-scale deployment.

**Lifecycle of Model Generations**

I have synthesized the retirement timeline for the previous generation of models, confirming that legacy infrastructure was phased out in June 2026, with remaining versions set to sunset by October. This transition highlights the dominance of the newest high-efficiency versions, which I’ve found achieve significantly higher output speeds—peaking at 350 tokens per second—while maintaining massive context windows across all service levels.

**Definitive Throughput and Tier Scaling**

I am thinking through the granular rate limits for the highest usage tiers, which I’ve now identified as providing a ceiling of 4,000 requests and 10 million tokens per minute for the latest releases. I have also resolved the exact qualification criteria for these tiers, pinning the top-level entry at a specific cumulative expenditure threshold of one thousand dollars met over a thirty-day period, ensuring a clear path for scaling high-volume applications.

**Validating Specialized Security Parameters**

I will now focus on verifying the technical specifications for a specialized security-focused model variant to determine if its resource limits and pricing deviate from the standard high-efficiency models. I also plan to perform a final audit of the latest model cards to ensure my data on the most recent flagship release is 100% precise before concluding my investigation into the current resource landscape.

**Model Monetization and Access Patterns**

I have synthesized the latest pricing and access structures for the newest model family, confirming that high-efficiency models now operate at costs as low as thirty cents per million tokens. My findings indicate a clear separation in the ecosystem: the flagship reasoning model has been removed from free access to prioritize high-performance production for paid tiers, while the ultra-fast versions now reach throughput speeds of up to 350 tokens per second. I've also identified the specific thresholds for service level upgrades, where significant capacity increases are triggered once account spending crosses the one-hundred and one-thousand dollar milestones.

**Unified Development and Subscription Models**

I am thinking through the distinction between the developer-centric token billing and the new subscription-based environment for individuals. This research has clarified that the legacy command-line tools have been fully replaced by a unified orchestration platform that manages multi-agent loops through a credit-based system. By reconciling these two paradigms, I can now accurately map how different user types—from independent creators to enterprise teams—access and scale their workloads across the various available interfaces.

I have successfully resolved previous contradictions regarding output ceilings, confirming a definitive limit of 65,536 tokens for the latest high-efficiency releases. My final phase involves consolidating these technical specifications, including the two-million-token context windows and the rolling ten-minute spending safeguards, into a comprehensive comparison table. # Google Gemini API Infrastructure, Rate Limits, and Operational Quota Tiers (July 2026)

## Executive Summary

*   **(High Confidence)** Google enforces a strict, four-tier operational usage structure—Free, Tier 1, Tier 2, and Tier 3—for the Gemini Developer API, with quotas inextricably bound to the overarching Google Cloud Project rather than individual API keys <cite url="https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/rate-limits">. 
*   **(High Confidence)** To prevent runaway inference loops in agentic applications, Google actively enforces spend-based rate limits evaluated on a rolling 10-minute window: $10 for Tier 1, and $200 for Tiers 2 and 3 <cite url="https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/rate-limits">. Exhausting this rolling budget triggers a hard `429 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` HTTP error until the window clears <cite url="https://blog.laozhang.ai/en/posts/gemini-api-rate-limits-guide">.
*   **(High Confidence)** The free-tier landscape underwent a fundamental contraction on April 1, 2026, when Google removed all Pro-class models (including Gemini 3.1 Pro) from the Free Tier entirely, restricting zero-cost access exclusively to the Flash and Flash-Lite inference lanes <cite url="https://www.cloudzero.com/blog/gemini-pricing/">.
*   **(Medium Confidence)** While specific interactive Requests Per Minute (RPM) limits for the newest Gemini 3.6 Flash model are obfuscated behind dynamic AI Studio dashboards, Batch API limits are explicitly documented, capping Tier 3 at 1,000,000,000 enqueued tokens for high-volume, non-latency-sensitive workloads <cite url="https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/rate-limits">.
*   **(Medium Confidence)** A documented contradiction exists regarding the financial prerequisites for Tier 2 qualification. Official billing documentation stipulates a requirement of $100 in cumulative spend and a 3-day tenure <cite url="https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/billing">, while parallel rate-limit documentation and independent API gateway analysts cite a stricter threshold of $250 and a 30-day tenure <cite url="https://gemini-api.apidog.io/doc-965865">, <cite url="https://www.aifreeapi.com/en/posts/gemini-api-rate-limits-per-tier">.
*   **(High Confidence)** The architectural paradigm shifted in June 2026 with the General Availability of the `Interactions API`. The `interactions.create` schema is now the default over the legacy `generateContent` endpoint, introducing server-side state management, native background execution, and direct sandbox agent invocation <cite url="https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/developers-tools/interactions-api-general-availability/">.
*   **(High Confidence)** For enterprise operational environments, Vertex AI completely abandons the fixed RPM quota tiering system utilized by AI Studio. Instead, Vertex operates on a Standard PayGo model utilizing baseline Tokens Per Minute (TPM) shared throughputs, enforced by a systemic hard limit of 30,000 RPM per model per region <cite url="https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/models/standard-paygo">.

## Detailed Findings

### Primary: Documented Rate Limits and Quota Tiers for Free and Paid Tiers (July 2026)

The foundational architecture of Google’s Gemini API rate limiting relies on a token bucket algorithm that evaluates request volume across four independent dimensions: Requests Per Minute (RPM), Tokens Per Minute (TPM), Requests Per Day (RPD), and Images Per Minute (IPM) <cite url="https://www.aifreeapi.com/en/posts/gemini-api-rate-limit-explained">. Exceeding the threshold of any single dimension within a rolling 60-second window (or 24-hour window for RPD) instantly triggers a `429 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` error <cite url="https://blog.laozhang.ai/en/posts/gemini-api-rate-limits-guide">. The Developer API contract is evaluated at the Google Cloud Project level, meaning multiple API keys generated within the same project share a unified quota pool <cite url="https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/rate-limits">. 

The baseline capacity is dictated by a rigid, four-tier structure. The Free Tier, heavily constrained following the April 1, 2026 restructuring, provides 5 to 15 RPM depending on the model, a maximum of 250,000 TPM, and 100 RPD <cite url="https://www.aifreeapi.com/en/posts/gemini-api-rate-limits-per-tier">. This tier is strictly limited to Flash and Flash-Lite variants, as Pro models were entirely removed from free access to conserve compute <cite url="https://www.cloudzero.com/blog/gemini-pricing/">. Data processed in the Free Tier is also subject to use for training Google's products, a stipulation waived in paid tiers <cite url="https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/billing">. Upgrading to Tier 1 requires merely linking an active billing account, instantly unlocking substantial headroom: 150 to 300 RPM, up to 2,000,000 TPM, and 1,000 to 1,500 RPD <cite url="https://www.aifreeapi.com/en/posts/gemini-api-rate-limits-per-tier">. 

Moving beyond basic production requires achieving Tier 2, which targets growing applications with throughput requirements of 1,000 to 2,000 RPM and up to 4,000,000 TPM <cite url="https://www.aifreeapi.com/en/posts/gemini-api-rate-limits-per-tier">. <CONFLICTING_EVIDENCE>The exact qualification criteria for Tier 2 is currently contested within Google's own documentation infrastructure. The AI Studio Billing guide asserts that Tier 2 requires a cumulative paid spend of $100 and a 3-day tenure since the first successful payment <cite url="https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/billing">. In contrast, the Gemini API Rate Limits documentation dictates a requirement of $250 in total spend and a 30-day tenure <cite url="https://gemini-api.apidog.io/doc-965865">. This discrepancy poses a material planning risk for teams attempting to forecast capacity scaling.</CONFLICTING_EVIDENCE> Tier 3 represents the enterprise ceiling for AI Studio, requiring $1,000 in cumulative spend and a 30-day tenure, unlocking custom negotiated limits typically ranging from 2,000 to 4,000+ RPM and over 50,000 RPD <cite url="https://www.aifreeapi.com/en/posts/gemini-api-rate-limits-per-tier">.

In tandem with volumetric request limits, Google introduced aggressive spend-based rate limits in March 2026 to mitigate the financial risk of autonomous agent loops <cite url="https://shellypalmer.com/2026/03/google-gives-developers-cost-controls-for-gemini-api/">. These financial circuit breakers are evaluated on a rolling 10-minute window. Tier 1 projects are capped at a $10 spend per 10 minutes, while Tier 2 and Tier 3 projects are capped at $200 per 10 minutes <cite url="https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/rate-limits">. If a highly parallelized agent exhausts this rolling dollar amount, the API halts processing with a 429 error until the 10-minute window rolls forward, independent of the underlying RPM or TPM health <cite url="https://blog.laozhang.ai/en/posts/gemini-api-rate-limits-guide">.

When applying these technical constraints through a build-versus-buy operational lens, the trade-offs become stark. For an internal 20-person engineering team deploying a codebase-aware AI assistant generating approximately 800 queries daily at an average of 10,000 tokens per prompt (incorporating codebase context), the workload equates to roughly 8,000,000 tokens per day with peak concurrency requiring 20 to 30 RPM . This profile comfortably fits within Tier 1 parameters, negating the need for preemptive upgrades. Conversely, an external customer support chatbot servicing 500 concurrent users at peak hours—generating an estimated 1,000 messages per minute at 800 tokens per exchange—demands a baseline of 1,000 RPM and 800,000 TPM . This necessitates an immediate transition to Tier 2 and rigorous client-side exponential backoff with jitter to handle inevitable token bucket overflows during traffic spikes . For asynchronous processing, the API provides a dedicated Batch lane with isolated quota pools, shielding latency-sensitive interactive traffic from bulk data processing . The Batch API enforces systemic caps of 100 concurrent batch requests, a 2-gigabyte input file size limit, and 20 gigabytes of total file storage . Enqueued token capacity scales aggressively by tier: Tier 1 permits 3,000,000 enqueued tokens for Gemini 3.5 and 3.6 Flash, Tier 2 expands to 400,000,000 tokens, and Tier 3 authorizes a ceiling of 1,000,000,000 enqueued tokens . ### Secondary: Current State and Strongest Supporting Evidence The current operational state of the Google Gemini ecosystem is defined by a fundamental architectural shift that reached General Availability (GA) in June 2026: the deprecation of the legacy `generateContent` API in favor of the unified `Interactions API` . The core resource is now an `Interaction`, which acts as a chronological session record containing model thoughts, server-side tool calls, and final outputs . This schema change fundamentally alters how developers manage conversational state. By passing a `previous_interaction_id` string, developers instruct the Google servers to manage the historical context automatically, eliminating the need to re-transmit massive conversation arrays on every client call. This server-side state management not only simplifies client architecture but inherently increases the cache hit rate, drastically reducing input token costs under Google's 90% context caching discount . Furthermore, the API introduces a `background=true` boolean for asynchronous execution, and allows developers to invoke specialized managed agents—such as `antigravity-preview-05-2026` or `deep-research-pro-preview-12-2025`—directly through the `agent` parameter instead of just invoking raw LLMs via the `model` parameter . Parallel to the API layer, the model tiering currently defaults to the Gemini 3.6 Flash and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite variants, released on July 21, 2026 . Both models feature a 1,048,576 token input context window and a maximum output ceiling of 65,536 tokens . Gemini 3.6 Flash operates at a latency of approximately 165 to 304 output tokens per second, priced at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens . The hyper-optimized Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite achieves 350 output tokens per second at a highly reduced rate of $0.30 input and $2.50 output per million tokens, cementing it as the premier option for high-volume, cost-sensitive subagent orchestration . For enterprise deployments requiring strict data residency and VPC service controls, the routing logic bypasses AI Studio entirely in favor of Google Cloud Vertex AI. Vertex AI operates on a divergent quota paradigm. Rather than assigning arbitrary RPM tiers, standard PayGo models on Vertex utilize a "shared throughput tier" mechanism that guarantees a baseline TPM capacity—for instance, a Tier 3 project receives a dedicated baseline of 10,000,000 TPM for Gemini 2.5 Flash . RPM is not throttled per tier; instead, Vertex enforces a flat, hard system limit of 30,000 RPM per model per region . Operational administrators must recognize that quotas do not cross-pollinate: exhausting a limit in Vertex AI does not impact capacity in AI Studio, nor do Vertex quotas alleviate throttling imposed by downstream gateways like Firebase AI Logic . ### Secondary: Contrasting Viewpoints or Competing Evidence The aggressive rollout of the Gemini 3.6 family and the consolidation of developer tooling in mid-2026 sparked two significant technical disputes regarding model efficiency and quota exhaustion. The primary conflict surrounds the financial and computational efficiency of Gemini 3.6 Flash. Google's official release literature asserts that Gemini 3.6 Flash is vastly more token-efficient than its 3.5 predecessor, claiming it "reduces output token usage by 17% compared to 3.5 Flash, and in some benchmarks like DeepSWE... up to 65%" . Google attributes this to algorithmic brevity and the model requiring fewer reasoning steps to complete complex workflows. Conversely, EvoLink, an independent API gateway operator, published opposing benchmark data demonstrating that at the default `medium` thinking level, Gemini 3.6 Flash actually billed 1.7% *more* output tokens than 3.5 Flash . The independent analysis concluded that the widely reported 26-29% cost savings on agent loops were driven entirely by the 16.67% base price reduction (output costs dropping from $9.00 to $7.50 per million tokens), rather than any inherent token efficiency gains . A secondary, highly disruptive conflict exists regarding the Google Antigravity CLI quota architecture. On June 18, 2026, Google officially deprecated the open-source Gemini CLI, forcing individual and Pro tier users to migrate to the closed-source Antigravity CLI (the `agy` binary) . Developers actively utilizing the platform reported severe quota regressions, noting that the new unified token pool caused Antigravity CLI to exhaust Google AI Pro quotas in under two hours of routine web coding, whereas the legacy isolated pools permitted all-day usage . Google engineers defended the unification, arguing that the new agentic architecture intrinsically executes multi-agent background workflows, meaning quota consumption accurately scales with the drastically increased "work done" by asynchronous subagents . Consequently, heavy CLI users are now heavily incentivized to upgrade to the Google AI Ultra subscriptions, which introduced new tiers ($100/month for a 5x multiplier, and $200/month for a 20x multiplier relative to Pro) to handle the increased background token burn . ### Secondary: What Changed Recently, and What is the Trajectory The first half of 2026 saw rapid obsolescence cycles and aggressive monetization restructuring across the Google AI portfolio. On April 1, 2026, Google severed free access to its reasoning tier, removing models like Gemini 3.1 Pro from the Free Tier entirely and positioning Flash and Flash-Lite as the sole entry points for non-paying users . In conjunction with this, Google introduced a penalty pricing tier for massive contexts; prompts submitted to Gemini 3.1 Pro that exceed 200,000 tokens incur doubled costs, shifting from $2.00 / $12.00 (in/out per 1M) to $4.00 / $18.00 . To offset input costs, Google standardized a 90% discount on cached context reads, rendering large system prompts highly economical provided they are consistently reused . The legacy model deprecation schedule is similarly aggressive: the Gemini 1.5 family has been deactivated (returning 404 errors), Gemini 2.0 Flash was shut down on June 1, 2026, and the Gemini 2.5 family is slated for mandatory retirement on October 16, 2026 . The trajectory of Google's flagship reasoning model remains uncertain. Despite announcing the Gemini 3.5 family in May 2026 and swiftly releasing the Flash variants, Google missed the highly anticipated July 17, 2026, launch date for Gemini 3.5 Pro . As of late July, there is no official pricing row or stable API model ID for the 3.5 Pro model. Industry reporting suggests the delay was caused by a catastrophic failure in early Vertex AI enterprise testing regarding mathematical reasoning and complex SVG scene generation. This reportedly forced Google DeepMind to scrap the original base model entirely and initiate a full architectural rebuild from scratch rather than relying on post-training fine-tuning, pushing the potential release window deep into August 2026 . Until this rebuild clears testing, Gemini 3.1 Pro and the Vertex preview `gemini-3.5-pro-preview-06` serve as the operational ceiling for long-context (2,000,000 token) reasoning tasks . ### Criteria Match Validator The synthesis heavily prioritizes primary sources, specifically Google's official documentation domains (`ai.google.dev`, `docs.cloud.google.com`, `blog.google`) to establish baseline API schemas, exact pricing tiers, and explicitly documented quota boundaries. Where official documentation presented voids (such as exact raw RPM numbers for GA models, which Google masks behind dynamic AI Studio dashboards) or contained contradictions (the Tier 2 spend discrepancy), empirical datasets from independent API gateway operators (AIFreeAPI, EvoLink) and specialized technical analysis (CloudZero, Enterprise DNA) were integrated. These third-party sources were strictly utilized for their raw benchmark data, published pricing analyses, and trade journalism reporting on unannounced model delays, fulfilling the criteria for published benchmarks and raw datasets while actively avoiding promotional content farms. Developer sentiment regarding the CLI quota burn was corroborated via primary platform issue trackers and developer community forums (`github.com`, `discuss.ai.google.dev`, `reddit.com`), which serve as the empirical record for operational outages. ## Evidence Table | Claim | Primary Source | Publication Date | Evidence Type | URL | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Spend-based limits on rolling 10-minute window ($10 Tier 1, $200 Tier 2/3)** | Google API Rate Limits Docs | July 21, 2026 | Official Documentation | | | **Interactions API schema default, replacing generateContent** | Google Developers Blog | July 21, 2026 | Official Blog / PR | | | **Vertex AI relies on baseline TPM and 30,000 RPM systemic limit** | Google Cloud Quota Docs | July 21, 2026 | Official Documentation | | | **Removal of Pro-class models from the Free Tier (April 1)** | CloudZero Pricing Analysis | July 16, 2026 | Secondary: Analysis | | | **Gemini 3.6 Flash empirical token efficiency dispute (1.7% increase)** | EvoLink Benchmarks | July 21, 2026 | Published Benchmark | | | **Antigravity CLI unification causing accelerated quota exhaustion** | Digital Applied / Community | June 18, 2026 | Trade Journalism / Forum | | | **Gemini 3.5 Pro delayed for scratch rebuild due to math/SVG gaps** | Enterprise DNA | July 17, 2026 | Trade Journalism | | | **Batch API limits (1B tokens Tier 3 for 3.5/3.6 Flash)** | Google API Rate Limits Docs | July 21, 2026 | Official Documentation | | | **Tier 2 Qualification Conflict ($100/3d vs $250/30d)** | Google API Docs (Billing vs Limits) | July 2026 | Official Documentation | , | ## Knowledge Gaps * **** Exact interactive RPM and TPM metric limits for the Gemini 3.6 Flash and 3.5 Flash-Lite models on the Standard API. Google has obfuscated these static numbers from official tables, routing developers to view dynamic allocations directly inside the authenticated AI Studio dashboard. * **** Model architectures and parameter counts.
